setting: a hallway in a mental hospital

Ms. O'Hara: an older woman who has short mousy brown hair in a wild mess at the top of her head. white as a ghost, and trying not to panic. small boned, with a sweet face. She is adorned in the blue pajamas in [Image1] and [Image2] that all of the patients wear and she is holding her arms perfectly straight and still at her side while two nurses, one on either side, buckle the straps to the stretcher they are wheeling her on. On her head she wears a metal helmet with many little wires hanging off of it. The wires are red and blue and gold.

the two nurses: a male nurse, asian man, mid thirties, wearing a white coat over navy nurses scrubs and a female nurse, jamaican, big boned.

title: Ms. O'Hara — the straps, "where are they taking you?"
text:
Sophie steps out of the doorway of her room and watches as the two nurses buckle the straps around her wrists.

"where are they taking you?" says sophie

“They say I have to get shock treatment." says ms o hara
"I don’t mind the treatment, I’m just worried about what it will do to my memory.


The doctor said I might not remember everything once I’ve had it,” she says, looking worried indeed.

title: Ms. O'Hara — clip A: the stretcher passes, "where are they taking you", her memory
text:
sophie sees ms o hara, a patient she's never seen before, being wheeled down the hallway past her room, on her way to get shock treatment.

she starts biting her nail as she sees the stretcher pass, getting increasingly agitated, then, against her better judgement, follows the stretcher down the hall at a slight distance, trailing uselessly behind, as the two nurses, having already strapped in her chest, fuss with the small buckles that strap down her wrist.

in a small voice, without really excepting her to answer, sophie asks, in spite of herself: "where are they taking you," slight panic and mounting apprehension making their way into her voice.

"i have to get shock treatment," says ms o hara, in a flat voice, with sheer terror just below the surface. sophie can tell she is trying to be brave, and tries not to show how much this bothers her.

"i don't mind the treatment so much," says ms o hara, wincing as they tighten the straps around her wrist. "i just don't like what it does to my memory," she says limply, her eyes looking off into some far off place, as though imagining the memory loss, her face blank, expressionless, her eyes hollow and distant. panic sitting just below the surface, as she struggles to keep her composure.

She points her face up at one of the nurses so he is forced to make eye contact with her. “Yees.” he says encouragingly, “To help your miiind Ms. O’Hara. To help you stop having those visions.” he draws out the word mind as if she might not quite undersand if he doesn’t.

As they begin wheeling her away, Sophie follows, reaching her hand out like she wants to help but can't.

“Shh Shh Ms. O’Hara. After your treatment, you’ll feel muuch better.” says the same male nurse. “Now we’ll just wheel you to the treatment room. 

Are you ready to be wheeled, Ms. O’Hara?” 
The woman nods, closing her eyes as they well with tears. She moves her hand to brush them away but it’s now fully strapped to the gurney and it simply falls limp at her side.

title: Walking beside the stretcher — be a good girl and go back to your room

title: The end of the hallway — take the pill / don't take the pill
status: ready — the door with no handle (a possible ending)
text: She sits at the end of the hallway, next to the hallway which patients go in as they choose. It’s never been locked so long as she’s been there but there is no handle on the inside of the door. mulling over the matter of whether or not to take the pill she’s been prescribed. “Take the pill,” she mutters, clenching her fists tightly, then releasing, and the antithesis: “Don’t take the pill,” she clenches her fists again. She repeats these two phrases eleven times in a row before screwing up her eyes in concentration as though the decision were laid out in front of her and she has just to interpret it in order to know what to do. She gives up and resorts to clenching her fists again, muttering those words over and over so it sounds like a mantra.
